title: The first verse
hookLine: same alarm, same cold coffee, same slow bus: a different day, because a different mind
tomorrow: can anger ever be ended by more anger?

cards: Some mornings the alarm, the cold coffee and the slow bus feel like a conspiracy. Other mornings the very same three things barely register. Same alarm.
Same coffee. Same bus. So which came first, the bad mood or the bad day?
The Dhammapada opens with its answer, and it's the first line of the whole collection: manopubbangama dhamma. Mind goes before.

teach.b: Mano: mind. Pubbangama: going before. Dhamma: here not the teaching, but things, states, whatever you experience.
Things have mind going ahead of them.

teach.h: AS THE WHEEL FOLLOWS THE OX.
teach.b: Max Müller's English stretches it out: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage."
The next verse is its mirror: act from a clear mind, and happiness follows like a shadow that never leaves. Now a neighbor who says something close.

teach.h: KEEP THY HEART WITH ALL DILIGENCE.
teach.b: The book of Proverbs, in the King James Bible, says: "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life."
Shared ground: both say what comes out of a life starts inside, and both say it's worth guarding. Two traditions, one human habit noticed from two directions.
One honest difference: Proverbs is a father teaching his son within a faith in God, and the heart is kept before God.
The Dhammapada describes cause and result, mind to act to what follows, the way a wheel follows an ox, without naming God at all.

how: Dhammapada study usually begins with its first pair of verses, and Theravada teachers use them to introduce the training of the mind.

o: the last words the Buddha ever said
the verse monks chant before meals
the opening verse: mind goes before

games.q: the first verse — tap the pairs.
p: out of the heart are the issues of life

s: dhamma always means the Buddha's teaching
in this verse it means things, states, whatever you experience.
in Dhammapada 1, pain follows like the wheel behind the ox
and verse 2 mirrors it: happiness follows like a shadow that never leaves.
the verse says your bad days are your fault
it describes cause and result, mind going first; it says nothing about blame.

games.q: two coworkers get the same rushed email from the boss. one fumes all afternoon; the other shrugs. by the first verse, what made the difference?
o: the mind each one brought to it went first.
the email was secretly harsher for one of them.
one was born calm, and that can never change.
games.why: manopubbangama dhamma: things have mind going before them. same email, different minds, different afternoons.

practice: Close your eyes and say the first line once, inwardly: manopubbangama dhamma. Then just watch for the very next thought, and the one after it, and notice whether each one has a mood riding in front of it.
Don't change anything; just see which goes first.

wordCard.voice: The first verse. Manopubbangama dhamma: mind goes before all things, and what follows follows it, like a wheel behind the ox. Word fifteen of a little Pali.

orig.note: manopubbangama dhamma in Devanagari letters: mind goes before things (Dhammapada 1).

carryVoice: Here's the line: mind goes before, so the morning starts a step earlier than the alarm. That's day fifteen.
